q: Your developer productivity agent's loop treats the task as finished whenever Claude's response contains a text block. Users report it stopping mid-task right after Claude writes "Let me check the config file next." What is the correct fix?
o: Keep looping while `stop_reason` is "tool_use" and stop only when `stop_reason` is "end_turn".
Raise the maximum iteration count so the agent has more chances to finish the work.
Tell Claude in the system prompt to write "TASK COMPLETE" when done, and loop until that phrase appears.
Strip text blocks from every response so the loop only ever sees tool calls.
e: `stop_reason` is the structured signal for loop control: "tool_use" means run the requested tool and continue, "end_turn" means Claude is done. Checking for assistant text as a completion signal is a named anti-pattern, because Claude often narrates while still calling tools. Magic phrases are natural-language parsing (also an anti-pattern), and raising the iteration cap doesn't fix the wrong termination test.

q: Claude asks to call `lookup_order`. Your code runs the tool and gets the result. What must happen before the next request to Claude?
o: Append Claude's tool_use message and a tool_result message to the conversation history, then send the full history.
Send only the tool result as a fresh user message and drop earlier turns to save tokens.
Summarize the tool result into the system prompt and restart the conversation from scratch.
Store the result in a database and give Claude a separate tool to query it later.
e: Tool results are appended to the conversation history so the model can reason about its next action with the new information. Dropping earlier turns breaks coherence (the model loses the request it was working on), and moving results into the system prompt or a database adds indirection the loop doesn't need.

q: A teammate proposes capping the agent loop at 5 iterations as the main way to stop it. What's the best assessment?
o: Keep a cap only as a safety backstop; the main stop signal should be `stop_reason` "end_turn", or long tasks get cut off.
Adopt it, since a fixed iteration cap is the standard and most predictable way to end an agentic loop.
Cap total output tokens instead, because tokens measure the work done more accurately than iterations.
Adopt it but raise the cap to 50, so it rarely triggers while still controlling when the loop ends.
e: The guide lists "setting arbitrary iteration caps as the primary stopping mechanism" as an anti-pattern. The model signals completion with `stop_reason` "end_turn". A cap of any size, or a token cap, is still an arbitrary limit pretending to be a completion signal.

q: Your support agent runs a hard-coded sequence for every request: get_customer → lookup_order → process_refund. It handles refunds well but fails on billing disputes and account issues. What's the better design?
o: Give Claude the tools with clear descriptions and let it pick the next tool from context, enforcing only critical prerequisites in code.
Add more branches to the decision tree so every request type (billing, account, refund) gets its own fixed sequence.
Train a classifier on past tickets to choose one of several pre-built tool sequences for each new request.
Call all four tools on every request so Claude always has complete data, and let it ignore what's irrelevant.
e: The guide contrasts model-driven decision-making (Claude reasons about which tool to call next) with pre-configured decision trees. High-ambiguity support requests need adaptive tool choice. More branches or a classifier just builds a bigger tree, and calling every tool wastes calls and can trigger actions (like refunds) that weren't wanted. Programmatic gates stay for rules that must always hold.

q: A response contains a text block ("I'll search for recent studies now") followed by a tool_use block, and `stop_reason` is "tool_use". What should the loop do?
o: Run the requested tool, append the result to the history, and continue the loop.
Show the text to the user and end the turn, since Claude produced a reply.
Ignore the tool_use block because the text shows Claude is still thinking.
Ask the end user to confirm every tool call before it runs.
e: `stop_reason` "tool_use" means Claude wants a tool executed and expects the result back. Text alongside the tool call is commentary, not a completion signal. Ending on text is the classic anti-pattern, and per-call user confirmation defeats an autonomous research pipeline.

q: In your research system, subagents message each other directly (search sends results straight to synthesis, synthesis asks search for more). Debugging is painful and errors are handled inconsistently. What should you change?
o: Route all subagent communication through the coordinator for observability, consistent error handling, and controlled flow.
Add a shared message bus that every subagent reads and writes, so messages are centralized without a coordinator.
Merge all the subagents into one large agent so there are no messages between agents left to debug.
Keep the direct connections but add detailed structured logging inside each subagent to trace messages.
e: Hub-and-spoke puts the coordinator in charge of all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and routing. That gives one place to observe, handle errors, and control what each agent sees. A shared bus or extra logging keeps the tangled flow, and merging everything loses specialization.

q: Your coordinator runs every query through search → analysis → synthesis → report, even simple factual questions like "When was this company founded?" Latency and cost are high. What's the best improvement?
o: Have the coordinator assess each query and choose which subagents to invoke.
Cache past answers so that repeated or similar questions can skip the full pipeline entirely.
Run all four subagents in parallel so the total latency drops to that of the slowest agent.
Remove the coordinator and let the search agent answer every incoming question directly.
e: The guide calls for coordinators that "dynamically select which subagents to invoke rather than always routing through the full pipeline." Caching helps only repeats, parallelism can't work when steps depend on each other, and removing the coordinator breaks complex queries that need the full pipeline.

q: Two web search subagents keep returning heavily overlapping sources for the same research topic. What's the most effective fix?
o: Partition the scope so each subagent gets distinct subtopics or source types.
Let both subagents run as they are, and have the synthesis agent remove duplicate sources afterwards.
Cut the system down to a single search subagent so there is nothing left to overlap.
Raise the temperature on one subagent so that its search queries drift away from the other's.
e: Partitioning scope (distinct subtopics or source types per agent) minimizes duplication at the source. Deduplicating later still wastes the duplicated work, one agent gives up parallel coverage, and temperature is a random nudge rather than a design.

q: The synthesis agent's draft report has thin coverage on two subtopics. Which pattern best fixes this inside the system?
o: An iterative refinement loop: the coordinator finds gaps, re-delegates targeted queries, and re-runs synthesis until coverage is sufficient.
Instruct the synthesis agent to fill any thin subtopics from its own training knowledge so the report is complete.
Rerun the entire pipeline from scratch with the same query, since a second pass usually finds different sources.
Add a clear disclaimer section to the report listing which subtopics may be incomplete so readers can follow up.
e: The guide describes exactly this loop: coordinator evaluates synthesis output for gaps, re-delegates with targeted queries, and re-invokes synthesis. Filling from training knowledge loses citations, rerunning the same query likely reproduces the same gaps, and a disclaimer documents the problem without fixing it.

q: For the topic "barriers to renewable energy adoption," the coordinator creates three subtasks: "solar panel costs," "solar permitting," and "solar grid integration." Every subagent succeeds, but the report ignores wind, storage, and policy. What is the root cause?
o: The coordinator's task decomposition is too narrow, so the assignments don't cover the topic's full scope.
The search subagent's queries aren't broad enough to find wind and storage sources.
The synthesis agent isn't told to identify coverage gaps in what it receives.
The analysis agent is filtering out non-solar documents with overly strict relevance rules.
e: The subagents did exactly what they were assigned; the assignments only covered solar. The guide warns about overly narrow decomposition by the coordinator leading to incomplete coverage. Blaming downstream agents misses that they worked correctly within the scope they were given.

q: You've defined AgentDefinitions for four subagents, but the coordinator never delegates and says it has no way to start other agents. What's the most likely cause?
o: The coordinator's `allowedTools` doesn't include "Task", the tool used to spawn subagents.
Each subagent must run on a separate server before the coordinator can reach it.
The subagent descriptions are too long for the coordinator to parse.
`tool_choice` must be set to "any" for delegation to work.
e: Subagents are spawned through the Task tool, and a coordinator can only call it if `allowedTools` includes "Task". Without it, the AgentDefinitions exist but nothing can invoke them. The other options aren't requirements for delegation.

q: The synthesis subagent writes reports that refer to "the findings above," but its output contains none of the actual search results. Why, and what's the fix?
o: Subagents don't inherit the coordinator's context; put the complete prior findings directly in the synthesis subagent's prompt.
Enable shared memory so every subagent can automatically read the results that other subagents produced.
Give the synthesis subagent a larger context window so the coordinator's full history fits inside it.
Let the synthesis subagent run its own web searches so it always has fresh material to cite in the report.
e: Subagents run with isolated context. They don't automatically inherit parent history or share memory, so context must be passed explicitly in the prompt. A bigger window doesn't help when the data was never sent, and letting synthesis search crosses roles.

q: When findings pass from the analysis subagent to synthesis, the final report loses track of which claim came from which document and page. What's the best fix?
o: Pass findings as structured data that keeps content separate from metadata such as URL, document name, and page.
Add a firm instruction to the synthesis agent's prompt reminding it to always cite the source of every claim.
Concatenate all findings into one text block, followed by a complete list of every source URL at the end.
Have the report agent run fresh searches after writing, to find and attach a source for each claim.
e: The guide recommends structured formats that separate content from metadata to preserve attribution between agents. A reminder can't recover metadata that was never passed, a trailing URL list breaks the claim-to-source link, and re-searching after the fact is slow and may attach the wrong sources.

q: Your coordinator spawns four independent search subagents one per turn, so the research phase takes about four times longer than one search. How do you parallelize it?
o: Have the coordinator emit multiple Task tool calls in a single response.
Switch the coordinator to a faster model.
Merge the four searches into one subagent that runs them in sequence.
Submit the four searches through the Message Batches API.
e: Parallel subagents come from emitting multiple Task tool calls in one coordinator response rather than across separate turns. A faster model doesn't remove sequencing, one merged agent is still sequential, and the Batches API has no latency guarantee and doesn't support multi-turn tool use.

q: The coordinator's prompt gives each subagent a rigid 15-step procedure ("search X, open the third result, extract paragraph two..."). Subagents fail whenever sources look different than expected. What's a better approach?
o: Specify research goals and quality criteria instead of procedures, so subagents can adapt to what they find.
Add more steps to the procedure that cover each edge case and source layout you've seen fail so far.
Add few-shot examples showing the exact click-by-click sequence each subagent should follow.
Hard-code the specific source URLs each subagent must use, so they never meet an unexpected layout.
e: The guide recommends coordinator prompts that "specify research goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedural instructions, to enable subagent adaptability." More steps, scripted examples, or fixed URLs make the procedure even more brittle.

q: You want a "test-writer" subagent that can read and write files but must never run Bash. Where is this best configured?
o: In its AgentDefinition: description, system prompt, and a tool list without Bash.
In the coordinator's system prompt, with a firm rule that it must never let the test-writer subagent run Bash commands.
In the project's CLAUDE.md, under a dedicated "test-writer rules" heading.
By forcing `tool_choice` to the Write tool on every single test-writer turn.
e: AgentDefinition holds each subagent type's description, system prompt, and tool restrictions. Restricting tools there is a hard limit. Prompt or CLAUDE.md instructions are only guidance, and forcing one tool every turn would stop it from reading files at all.

q: You invoke the document analysis subagent for paper A, then later invoke it again for paper B and ask it to compare B with A. It has no idea what A said. Why?
o: Subagents don't share memory between invocations; include paper A's analysis in the prompt.
It's a bug: subagents of the same type are supposed to remember their earlier invocations automatically.
The second invocation needs a larger context window so it can hold both papers at once.
You need to fork the first subagent's session instead of invoking the subagent a second time.
e: Each subagent invocation starts with only what its prompt contains. Subagents don't inherit parent context or share memory between invocations, so the coordinator must pass paper A's findings explicitly.

q: Policy requires identity verification before any account change. The system prompt says so clearly, yet audits show about 3% of account changes happen without verification. What's the most effective fix?
o: Add a programmatic gate that blocks account-change tools until verification returns a verified ID.
Repeat the verification rule in capital letters at both the start and the end of the system prompt.
Add several few-shot examples that show the agent always verifying identity before any account change.
Lower the temperature so the agent follows its system prompt instructions more consistently.
e: When compliance must be deterministic, prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate. A programmatic gate guarantees ordering. Emphasis, examples, and temperature all still rely on probabilistic compliance.

q: Which statement best describes prompt-based guidance for workflow steps that must always happen in order?
o: Prompts have a non-zero failure rate, so when compliance must be deterministic, enforce ordering in code.
A carefully written prompt achieves effectively 100% compliance, so code-level enforcement adds nothing.
Prompt guidance is preferable because it lets the model make sensible exceptions when a situation calls for it.
Hooks are mainly intended for logging and auditing, so prompts remain the right place for ordering rules.
e: The guide draws a clear line: programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) gives guarantees, while prompt-based guidance is probabilistic. For things like identity checks before financial operations, the failure rate of prompts alone isn't acceptable.

q: Mid-conversation, the agent must escalate a billing dispute to a human agent who cannot see the transcript. What should the handoff contain?
o: A structured summary: customer ID, root cause, amounts, what was tried, and the recommended action.
A copy of the customer's last three messages, so the human agent hears the problem in the customer's words.
A short note such as "Customer needs help with a billing dispute, please take over from here."
The customer's sentiment score and the agent's confidence rating, so the human can prioritize the case.
e: Structured handoff protocols include customer details, root cause analysis, and recommended actions, so a human without the transcript can act immediately. A few raw messages or a one-liner force the human to start over, and sentiment or confidence scores don't tell them what to do.

q: A customer writes: "My order arrived damaged, I was charged twice for it, and I need to change my shipping address." How should the agent handle this?
o: Split it into three items, investigate each with shared context, and give one unified resolution.
Resolve the first issue fully, then ask the customer to open separate tickets for the other two issues.
Escalate the whole conversation to a human, because requests with several issues are too complex to automate.
Handle only the most urgent issue (the double charge) now, and schedule a follow-up for the remaining ones.
e: The guide's pattern is to decompose multi-concern requests into distinct items, investigate each using shared context, and synthesize one unified resolution. Pushing issues to new tickets or dropping them hurts first-contact resolution, and multiple simple issues aren't a reason to escalate.

q: Your gate blocks `process_refund` until `get_customer` returns a verified ID. Claude tries `process_refund` first. What should the gate do?
o: Block the call and return an error saying verification via `get_customer` is required, so the agent can verify and retry.
Allow the refund to go through, but write a warning to the audit log so the team can review it later.
End the whole session immediately, so there is no chance of an unverified refund being processed.
Hand the conversation to a human agent right away, since the agent has already tried to break policy.
e: A prerequisite gate blocks the downstream call and tells the agent why, so it can complete the missing step and continue. Letting it through defeats the gate, and ending the session or escalating overreacts to something the agent can fix in its next step.

q: Refunds now require a verified customer, but audits find refunds issued on orders that belong to a different customer than the one verified. What's the most reliable fix?
o: Extend the programmatic prerequisite so `process_refund` is blocked unless the order's customer ID matches the verified customer ID.
Add a system prompt rule telling the agent to check that the order belongs to the customer.
Add few-shot examples where the agent notices mismatched orders.
Ask the customer to confirm the order number twice before refunding.
e: This is a business rule with financial consequences, so it belongs in code where it's guaranteed. Prompt rules and examples reduce the rate but can't eliminate it, and asking twice doesn't verify ownership.

q: Your MCP tools return dates as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, and "MM/DD/YY". The agent sometimes misreads them and miscalculates return windows. What's the best fix?
o: Add a PostToolUse hook that normalizes every date to one format before the model sees it.
Explain all three date formats in detail in the system prompt, with examples of each one.
Ask the model to convert every date it receives to ISO 8601 before it reasons about return windows.
Rewrite every backend service so they all return dates in the same format.
e: PostToolUse hooks intercept tool results and transform them before the model processes them, which is the guide's example for normalizing heterogeneous formats like Unix timestamps and ISO 8601. Prompt explanations are probabilistic, and rewriting every backend is far more work than needed.

q: Business rule: refunds over $500 must go to a human. Which implementation is most reliable?
o: A hook that intercepts outgoing `process_refund` calls over $500 and redirects to `escalate_to_human`.
A clear system prompt rule stating that any refund over $500 must be escalated to a human agent.
A PostToolUse hook that checks each refund right after it's processed and flags any that are over $500 for review.
Few-shot examples showing the agent escalating large refunds.
e: Intercepting the outgoing tool call blocks the policy-violating action before it happens and redirects to escalation. A PostToolUse check runs after the refund is already issued. Prompt rules and examples are probabilistic, which isn't enough for a hard financial limit.

q: The order tool returns a numeric status (1, 2, 3). The agent sometimes reads 3 as "shipped" when it means "cancelled." What's the best fix?
o: Use a PostToolUse hook to turn numeric status codes into descriptive labels before the model sees them.
Add a lookup table to the system prompt that explains what each numeric status code means.
Have the agent ask customers to confirm their order status before it takes any action on the order.
Remove the status field from the tool output so the agent can't misread it in the first place.
e: Normalizing numeric status codes is one of the guide's PostToolUse examples. Converting codes to clear labels removes the ambiguity entirely. A lookup table still relies on the model applying it correctly, and removing the field throws away information the agent needs.

q: When should you choose a hook over a prompt instruction?
o: When the rule needs guaranteed compliance; hooks are deterministic, prompts are probabilistic.
Always; every piece of guidance should be written as a hook so that agent behavior is fully predictable in every case.
Only for formatting changes; policy and business rules belong in the system prompt.
Only once the prompt has grown too long to hold any more instructions.
e: The guide distinguishes hooks for deterministic guarantees from prompts for probabilistic compliance, and says to choose hooks when business rules require guaranteed compliance. Turning all guidance into hooks removes the model's useful judgment, and prompt length isn't the deciding factor.

q: Your developer productivity agent must never run destructive commands like `rm -rf` or write outside the repository. What's the most reliable safeguard?
o: A hook that intercepts outgoing Bash and Write calls and blocks any that violate the policy.
A clear warning about destructive commands in CLAUDE.md.
A PostToolUse hook that detects destructive commands after they run and restores files.
An instruction for the model to double-check every command before running it.
e: Intercepting tool calls before they execute gives a deterministic guarantee. CLAUDE.md warnings and self-checks are probabilistic, and a PostToolUse hook runs after the damage is done.

q: Your CI review always checks the same aspects in order: security, then performance, then error handling, then a summary. Which decomposition pattern fits best?
o: Prompt chaining: a fixed sequential pipeline of focused steps.
Dynamic adaptive decomposition that creates new subtasks from what each step finds.
One large prompt that checks every aspect at once.
A separate model instance reviewing each line of code.
e: The guide recommends prompt chaining for predictable multi-aspect reviews and dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigation. The aspects here are known in advance, so a fixed chain of focused passes fits.

q: An engineer asks your agent to "add comprehensive tests to this legacy codebase." What's the best way to decompose this?
o: Map the structure first, find high-impact areas, then build a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies appear.
Generate tests file by file in alphabetical order until every file in the codebase has at least one test.
Use a fixed pipeline that writes one unit test for every function across the codebase, in a single pass.
Ask for 100% coverage in one detailed prompt and let the model decide how to work through the codebase.
e: This is the guide's own example of an open-ended task: map structure, find high-impact areas, build a prioritized plan that adapts as you learn. Alphabetical or one-test-per-function pipelines ignore impact, and a single prompt gives no structure.

q: An agent is investigating an intermittent production bug with an unknown cause. Which decomposition approach fits?
o: Dynamic adaptive decomposition, generating the next subtasks from what each step discovers.
A fixed sequence of predetermined diagnostic steps run in the same order every time.
A single prompt asking for the root cause directly.
Splitting the codebase evenly and assigning each part to its own subagent.
e: Open-ended investigations benefit from adaptive plans that generate subtasks based on what's found. A fixed sequence can't follow unexpected leads, and splitting the codebase blindly ignores where the evidence points.

q: Per-file review passes catch local issues, but they miss a bug where file A changes a function's signature while file B still calls it the old way. What should you add?
o: A separate cross-file integration pass that examines data flow between the changed files.
More detailed per-file instructions about checking function calls.
A larger context window for each per-file pass.
A request for the developer to list cross-file dependencies in the PR description.
e: The guide's pattern is per-file local analysis plus a separate cross-file integration pass. Per-file passes by design can't see the mismatch between two files, and a bigger window per file doesn't help when the other file isn't in that pass.

q: You've spent 30 minutes building a shared analysis of a codebase and want to compare two refactoring approaches without one contaminating the other. What should you do?
o: Use `fork_session` to create two independent branches from the shared analysis baseline.
Try approach A in the current session, revert, then try approach B in the same session.
Start two new sessions and redo the analysis in each.
Run /compact, then try both approaches one after the other.
e: `fork_session` creates independent branches from a shared baseline to explore divergent approaches. Reusing one session leaves approach A's reasoning in context while trying B, and redoing the analysis wastes the 30 minutes you already invested.

q: Yesterday you ran a named investigation session called "auth-refactor." How do you pick it up today?
o: `claude --resume auth-refactor`
`claude -p "continue auth-refactor"`
Start a new session and paste in yesterday's final message.
`/compact auth-refactor`
e: Named session resumption uses `--resume <session-name>`. `-p` runs a new non-interactive prompt, pasting one message loses most of the context, and /compact summarizes the current session rather than loading another.

q: You resume a session after teammates changed three of the files it analyzed earlier. What's the best next step?
o: Tell the resumed session exactly which files changed so it re-analyzes just those.
Carry on as if nothing changed; the session will notice when it reads the files again.
Ask it to re-explore the entire codebase from scratch.
Delete the session and start over without context.
e: The guide says to inform a resumed session about specific file changes for targeted re-analysis rather than full re-exploration. Saying nothing risks reasoning from stale results, and starting over throws away context that's still valid.

q: After a week of heavy changes, most tool results in your old session are stale. What's the most reliable way to continue?
o: Start a new session and inject a structured summary of the key findings that still hold.
Resume the old session and keep working.
Resume the old session and run /compact first.
Fork the old session and continue in the fork.
e: When prior tool results are stale, starting fresh with an injected summary is more reliable than resuming. Resuming, compacting, or forking all carry the stale results forward.

q: When is resuming a prior session the better choice than starting fresh with a summary?
o: When most of the prior context is still valid, for example the code hasn't changed much.
Always, because resuming keeps more information than any summary could.
Only when the previous session was shorter than about 10 minutes.
Never, because starting fresh with a summary is always more reliable.
e: The guide's rule: resume when prior context is mostly valid, start fresh with an injected summary when tool results are stale. Neither "always" nor "never" is right, and session length isn't the criterion.

q: In a hub-and-spoke multi-agent system, which responsibilities belong to the coordinator?
o: Decomposition, delegation, aggregation, choosing subagents, and routing information and errors between them.
Only combining the final results, while subagents decide among themselves which agent to call next.
Running all the web searches itself, while the subagents only format and polish the final output.
Starting the first subagent in the pipeline, then stepping aside while the subagents hand off work.
e: The coordinator manages decomposition, delegation, aggregation, subagent selection, and all inter-subagent communication and error handling. Letting subagents route among themselves breaks the hub-and-spoke model.

q: Your agent runs requested tools but never adds their results back to the conversation. Claude keeps asking for the same tool over and over. What's wrong?
o: Tool results must be appended to the history so Claude can use them in its next step.
Claude needs a higher `max_tokens` value so that it has enough room left to process each tool result fully.
`tool_choice` should be set to "auto", which stops Claude from repeating the same tool call.
The tool's description should say it only ever needs to be called once.
e: Without the tool result in context, Claude never learns the outcome and reasonably asks again. Appending results between iterations is how the model incorporates new information. The other options don't address the missing result.

q: The coordinator returns a response with `stop_reason` "end_turn" containing the final cited report. What should your loop do?
o: Exit the loop and deliver the final response.
Send "Are you sure you're done?" and run one more iteration.
Check the text for the word "done" before deciding.
Call the synthesis subagent again to double-check the report.
e: "end_turn" is the signal that Claude has finished. Extra confirmation turns or keyword checks add natural-language parsing and cost without improving reliability. Quality review, if needed, is a deliberate design step, not a loop-termination check.

q: Your research system has `analyze_content` and `analyze_document` with nearly identical descriptions. The agent often sends web search results to `analyze_document`. What's the best fix?
o: Rename `analyze_content` to `extract_web_results` with a web-specific description that sets it apart.
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing which of the two tools to pick for web results.
Merge the two tools into one and let the backend decide internally which analysis logic to run.
Add a line to the system prompt telling the agent to read tool descriptions carefully before choosing.
e: Overlapping names and descriptions cause misrouting. The guide's own fix is renaming `analyze_content` to `extract_web_results` with a web-specific description. Examples and generic reminders work around the root cause, and merging hides two different jobs behind one interface.

q: Which content makes a tool description most effective for reliable tool selection?
o: Input formats, example queries, edge cases, and when to use it versus similar tools.
Just the function signature, since well-chosen parameter names already explain what the tool does.
Internal implementation details such as the database tables and service endpoints the tool calls.
A one-line summary, to keep token use low.
e: Tool descriptions are the main way the model chooses tools, and the guide lists input formats, example queries, edge cases, and boundary explanations as what to include. Minimal descriptions lead to unreliable selection, and backend internals don't help the model decide when to use the tool.

q: A generic `analyze_document` tool is used for data extraction, summarization, and claim verification, and its outputs are inconsistent across these uses. What's the best redesign?
o: Split it into `extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, and `verify_claim_against_source`, each with its own contract.
Keep one tool but add a free-text `mode` parameter that tells it whether to extract, summarize, or verify.
Keep one tool but rewrite its description at much greater length, covering all three uses in detail.
Keep one tool and add few-shot examples to the prompt showing correct calls for each of the three uses.
e: The guide recommends splitting generic tools into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts, using exactly this example. A free-text mode or a longer description keeps one fuzzy interface doing three jobs.

q: Your system prompt says: "Whenever the customer mentions their account, look up their details first." Now the agent calls `get_customer` for questions like "What's the status of the order on my account?" instead of `lookup_order`. What's the root cause?
o: A keyword-triggered instruction in the system prompt creates a tool association that overrides the descriptions.
The `lookup_order` description is too long, so the model skims it and falls back on `get_customer`.
The sampling temperature is set too high, which makes the model's tool choices partly random.
The agent needs a third tool that looks up customers and orders together in a single call.
e: The guide warns that keyword-sensitive system prompt wording can create unintended tool associations that override good tool descriptions. The fix is to review and reword the instruction. Temperature or a combined tool doesn't address the trigger word.

q: What is the primary mechanism Claude uses to decide which tool to call?
o: The tool descriptions.
The alphabetical order of tool names.
The position of each tool in the tools list.
The number of parameters each tool takes.
e: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection, which is why minimal or overlapping descriptions lead to misrouting.

q: Your agent has `search_code` ("Searches") and `search_docs` ("Searches documents"). It often picks `search_docs` for questions about functions in the code. What's the best first step?
o: Expand both descriptions to state purpose, inputs, outputs, and when to use each.
Build a routing layer that scans each query for code keywords and pre-selects the right tool before Claude sees it.
Merge both tools into a single `search` tool that searches code and docs together.
Remove `search_docs` so the agent can only search code.
e: Minimal descriptions are the root cause, and clear, differentiated descriptions are the low-effort, high-leverage first fix. A routing layer is over-engineered, and merging or removing tools gives up a real distinction.

q: When `process_refund` hits a policy violation, your MCP tool returns "Operation failed." The agent retries five times and then tells the customer to try later. What's the best fix?
o: Return a structured error: `isError`, a business category, `isRetryable: false`, and a customer-friendly reason.
Return an empty result instead of an error, so the agent moves on without retrying the failed refund.
Throw an exception from the tool that ends the session, so the agent can't keep retrying the refund.
Add a rule to the system prompt saying the agent must never retry any tool more than twice in a row.
e: Generic errors stop the agent from choosing the right recovery. Structured metadata (category, retryable flag, readable explanation) tells it not to retry and gives it words for the customer. A retry cap in the prompt still wastes attempts and still leaves the customer misinformed.

q: How should an MCP tool tell the agent that a call failed?
o: Set the `isError` flag on the tool result, ideally with structured details.
Return an HTTP 500 status code so the agent framework knows the call failed.
Return an empty string as the result so the agent sees that nothing came back.
Put the word "ERROR" at the very start of an otherwise normal text result.
e: MCP uses the `isError` flag pattern to communicate tool failures back to the agent. An empty result can look like a valid "no matches" result, and text conventions are unreliable.

q: `lookup_order` times out because the order service is briefly unavailable. Which structured error fits best?
o: `errorCategory: "transient"` with `isRetryable: true`
`errorCategory: "validation"` with `isRetryable: false`
`errorCategory: "permission"` with `isRetryable: false`
`errorCategory: "business"` with `isRetryable: false`
e: Timeouts and brief service outages are transient errors and are worth retrying. Validation errors are bad input, permission errors are access problems, and business errors are policy violations; none of those succeed on retry.

q: A customer asks to return an item bought 45 days ago, outside the 30-day window. `process_refund` rejects it. What should the tool return?
o: A business-rule error with `retriable: false` and a customer-friendly explanation to pass along.
A transient error with `isRetryable: true`, so the agent tries the refund again in a moment.
A generic "Operation failed" message, so internal policy details aren't exposed to the agent.
An empty success response, so the conversation flow isn't interrupted by an error.
e: Business rule violations are non-retryable. The guide recommends `retriable: false` plus a customer-friendly explanation so the agent communicates the policy well. Marking it transient causes pointless retries, and a fake success misleads everyone.

q: The web search subagent hits a transient timeout. Where should this be handled first?
o: Retry locally inside the subagent first; if that fails, report to the coordinator with partial results and what was tried.
Send every error straight to the coordinator immediately, however minor, so it has full visibility.
Suppress the timeout and return the results gathered so far, marked as a complete and successful search.
End the whole research workflow, so an incomplete report is never produced from partial data.
e: The guide recommends local recovery within subagents for transient failures, propagating only unresolved errors along with partial results and what was tried. Suppressing errors and aborting everything are both named anti-patterns.

q: `get_customer` finds no customer for the email provided, and the agent tells the customer "our system is down right now." What's the fix?
o: Have the tool distinguish a valid empty result (no match found) from an access failure.
Treat every empty result as an error, so the agent stays cautious about missing data.
Make the agent retry the lookup three times before it says anything to the customer.
Escalate the conversation to a human whenever a customer lookup returns nothing.
e: A successful query with no matches is valid information (maybe the customer used another email). Distinguishing it from an access failure lets the agent ask for another identifier instead of inventing an outage or retrying pointlessly.

q: Your synthesis agent has access to 18 tools, including web search and file operations. Tool selection has gotten worse, and it has started running its own web searches. What's the best fix?
o: Restrict each subagent to the 4–5 tools its role needs.
Write a stronger system prompt telling it to stay in its lane.
Set `tool_choice` to "any".
Move the synthesis agent to a larger model.
e: Too many tools (like 18 instead of 4–5) degrade selection, and agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them. Scoping tools to the role fixes both. Prompts and model size don't remove the temptation or the decision load.

q: The document analysis subagent uses a generic `fetch_url` tool and sometimes pulls in unrelated web pages. What's the best change?
o: Replace `fetch_url` with a constrained `load_document` tool that validates document URLs.
Tell the subagent in its prompt to fetch only documents.
Remove the fetch tool and paste every document into the prompt by hand.
Add a second fetch tool for web pages so it has a choice.
e: The guide's example is replacing a generic `fetch_url` with `load_document` that validates document URLs. Constraining the tool enforces the boundary, while a prompt only asks nicely.

q: You need `extract_metadata` to run before any enrichment tools on every document. How do you guarantee it?
o: Force it on the first turn with `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}`, then enrich in later turns.
Set `tool_choice` to "any" on the first turn, which guarantees that a tool call happens before anything else.
Keep `tool_choice` as "auto" and state clearly in the prompt that `extract_metadata` must always run first.
Put `extract_metadata` first in the tools array, since the model checks tools in the order they're listed.
e: Forced tool selection guarantees a specific tool runs. "any" guarantees some tool but not which one, "auto" lets the model choose or reply in text, and list order isn't a guarantee.

q: At one step of your workflow the agent must call one of several tools, but sometimes it replies with conversational text instead. Which setting fixes this while still letting it choose the right tool?
o: `tool_choice: "any"`
`tool_choice: "auto"`
`tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "get_customer"}`
A lower `max_tokens` value.
e: "any" requires the model to call a tool but lets it pick which. "auto" allows plain text, forcing one named tool removes the choice, and `max_tokens` doesn't control whether a tool is called.

q: Your productivity agent has one generic `run_anything` tool that executes arbitrary shell commands, and security review is worried. What's the best direction?
o: Replace it with constrained, purpose-specific tools (such as `run_tests`, `run_linter`) that validate inputs.
Keep the tool, but add a system prompt section asking the agent to be careful with shell commands.
Keep the tool, but log every command it runs so security can audit usage after the fact.
Remove all command execution from the agent, so it can only read and suggest code changes.
e: The guide recommends replacing generic tools with constrained alternatives. Purpose-specific tools with validated inputs narrow what can happen. Prompts and logs don't prevent misuse, and removing all execution makes the agent far less useful.

q: Your single agent has 5 tools and you plan to add 15 more MCP tools to it. What's the main risk?
o: More tools make selection harder and less reliable; spread them across specialized subagents.
Each additional tool adds network latency to every single tool call the agent makes.
The API rejects requests that define more than 10 tools, so the change will simply fail.
There's little risk, since a larger toolset gives the agent more capability to draw on.
e: The guide says giving an agent too many tools (18 instead of 4–5) degrades selection reliability. Distributing tools across role-scoped agents keeps each decision manageable.

q: Your team wants to share a GitHub MCP server through the repository without committing the access token. What's the right setup?
o: Configure it in the project's `.mcp.json` with environment variable expansion such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`.
Put the token directly in `.mcp.json` and keep the repository private so only the team can see it.
Have each developer add the server, with their own token, to their personal `~/.claude.json`.
Store the token in the project's CLAUDE.md so Claude can find it and pass it to the server.
e: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` is for shared team tooling, and environment variable expansion keeps credentials out of version control. User-level config isn't shared, and committing tokens (even in a private repository or CLAUDE.md) leaks secrets.

q: You want to try a new experimental MCP server just for yourself, without teammates getting it. Where should you configure it?
o: In your user-level `~/.claude.json`.
In the project's `.mcp.json`.
In `.claude/commands/`.
In the project's root CLAUDE.md.
e: User-level `~/.claude.json` is for personal or experimental servers. Project-level `.mcp.json` is shared with everyone via version control, and commands or CLAUDE.md don't configure MCP servers.

q: You have a shared server in `.mcp.json` and a personal one in `~/.claude.json`. Which tools can the agent use?
o: Tools from all configured servers, discovered at connection time and available at the same time.
Only the project server's tools; user-level servers are ignored inside a project.
Only one server at a time, so you switch between them manually.
Only the user-level server's tools, because user config overrides project config.
e: Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered at connection time and available simultaneously.

q: You added an MCP code-search tool that understands symbols and call graphs, but the agent keeps using the built-in Grep instead. What's the best fix?
o: Expand the MCP tool's description to explain in detail what it can do and what it returns.
Disable the built-in Grep tool so the agent has no choice but to use the MCP tool.
Rename the MCP tool to "grep" so the agent associates it with code searching.
Add a line to every prompt telling the agent it must use the MCP tool for searches.
e: The guide recommends enhancing MCP tool descriptions to explain capabilities and outputs in detail so the agent doesn't default to built-in tools. Disabling Grep removes a useful tool, and renaming creates confusion.

q: Your team needs Claude to work with Jira issues. What approach does the guide recommend?
o: Use an existing community MCP server for Jira, and keep custom servers for team-specific workflows.
Build your own custom Jira MCP server so you control every detail of the integration.
Paste a fresh export of Jira issues into CLAUDE.md every morning so Claude can read it.
Let the agent call the Jira web UI through Bash and curl whenever it needs issue data.
e: For standard integrations like Jira, choose existing community MCP servers and reserve custom servers for team-specific needs. Custom builds take more effort to write and maintain.

q: Your agents spend many tool calls just finding out what documentation and data sources exist before doing real work. What's the best improvement?
o: Expose the content catalog, such as the documentation hierarchy, as MCP resources.
Add more specialized search tools so the agents can explore the sources faster.
Paste the full documentation into every agent's system prompt so nothing needs finding.
Raise the iteration limit so the exploratory calls have room to finish before real work.
e: MCP resources expose content catalogs like documentation hierarchies, issue summaries, or database schemas, giving agents visibility into available data without exploratory tool calls. Pasting everything into the prompt wastes context.

q: You need to find every place in the codebase that calls `processPayment`. Which built-in tool fits best?
o: Grep
Glob
Read
Write
e: Grep searches file contents for patterns like function names, error messages, and imports. Glob matches file paths, not contents.

q: You need a list of every test file matching `**/*.test.tsx`. Which built-in tool fits best?
o: Glob
Grep
Read
Edit
e: Glob does file path pattern matching, finding files by name or extension. Grep searches inside files.

q: Claude's Edit call fails because the text it's anchoring on appears several times in the file. What's the reliable fallback?
o: Read the full file, then Write the modified version.
Retry the same Edit until it works.
Run a global find-and-replace with sed in Bash.
Grep for the text, then give up on the change.
e: Edit needs a unique text match. When it can't find one, the guide's fallback is Read + Write. Retrying fails the same way, and a global replace may change occurrences you didn't mean to.

q: An engineer asks the agent to explain how an unfamiliar codebase handles authentication. What's the best exploration strategy?
o: Grep for entry points, then Read files to follow imports and trace the flow.
Read every file in the repository first so the answer is based on complete information.
Glob for all files in the repository and Read them one by one in alphabetical order.
Answer from typical authentication patterns, without reading the code.
e: The guide recommends building understanding incrementally: Grep for entry points, then Read to follow imports and trace flows, instead of reading everything upfront. Reading all files wastes context, and guessing from typical patterns is unreliable.

q: `utils/index.ts` re-exports several helpers under new names. You need to find every use of these helpers across the codebase. What's the best approach?
o: List every name the wrapper module exports, then Grep for each name across the codebase.
Grep for the helpers' original function names, since aliases still point to the same functions.
Glob for every file that imports from `utils` and assume those are all the call sites.
Read `utils/index.ts` closely and trace usage from the definitions inside that one file.
e: Tracing usage across wrapper modules means identifying all exported names first, then searching for each one. Searching only the original names misses calls through the re-exported aliases.

q: A new team member's Claude Code sessions ignore the team's coding standards, while everyone else's follow them. The standards live in a senior developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. What's the fix?
o: Move the standards into the project-level CLAUDE.md in the repository so everyone gets them through version control.
Ask the new member to copy the senior developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` onto their machine.
Add the standards to the new member's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` only.
Put the standards in `.mcp.json` so they load with the MCP servers.
e: User-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` applies only to that user and isn't shared via version control. Team standards belong at project level. Copying files around by hand drifts over time, and `.mcp.json` configures MCP servers, not instructions.

q: In a monorepo, each package needs a different subset of the team's standards files (API, frontend, data). What's the most maintainable setup?
o: Use `@import` in each package's CLAUDE.md to pull in only the standards files that package needs.
Copy the relevant standards text into each package's CLAUDE.md.
Put every standard in the root CLAUDE.md and let Claude work out which applies.
Create a skill for each standard and invoke them manually.
e: The `@import` syntax keeps CLAUDE.md modular by referencing external files, and maintainers can choose which standards each package imports. Copying text duplicates it, and one giant root file loads irrelevant rules everywhere.

q: Your root CLAUDE.md has grown to 1,500 lines covering testing, API conventions, and deployment, and it's hard to maintain. What's the recommended restructuring?
o: Split it into focused topic files in `.claude/rules/`, such as `testing.md` and `deployment.md`.
Shorten it by deleting older rules until it fits in a few hundred lines.
Move the whole file to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` so it no longer clutters the repository.
Turn each section into a slash command that developers run when they need it.
e: `.claude/rules/` is for organizing topic-specific rule files as an alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md. Moving it to user level stops sharing it, and slash commands are on-demand workflows, not always-on standards.

q: Claude follows your conventions in some sessions but not others. You want to see which memory files are actually loaded. Which command helps?
o: `/memory`
`/compact`
`--resume`
e: The `/memory` command shows which memory files are loaded, which helps diagnose inconsistent behavior across sessions. `/compact` shrinks context, `--resume` continues a session, and `-p` runs non-interactively.

q: What are the three levels of the CLAUDE.md hierarchy?
o: User, project, and directory (subdirectory) CLAUDE.md files.
Global, organization, and team CLAUDE.md files.
System, user, and session CLAUDE.md files.
Project, branch, and commit CLAUDE.md files.
e: The guide lists user-level, project-level, and directory-level CLAUDE.md files. The other sets of levels aren't part of Claude Code's configuration hierarchy.

q: You want Claude to always explain its changes in more detail, but only for you, not your teammates. Where should this go?
o: In your user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
In the project root CLAUDE.md.
In a `.claude/rules/` file with `paths: ["**/*"]`.
In `.claude/commands/explain.md`.
e: User-level instructions apply only to you and aren't shared. Project CLAUDE.md and `.claude/rules/` are committed and affect everyone, and a command only runs when invoked.

q: You want a personal `/standup` command that summarizes your recent commits. Teammates don't need it. Where should it live?
o: `~/.claude/commands/`
`.claude/commands/` in the repository
The project root CLAUDE.md
`.mcp.json`
e: User-scoped commands go in `~/.claude/commands/` and stay personal. `.claude/commands/` in the repository is shared with the team via version control.

q: Your codebase-analysis skill produces pages of verbose output that crowd the main conversation. What should you add to its SKILL.md frontmatter?
o: `context: fork`, so it runs in an isolated sub-agent context.
`allowed-tools: Read`, so the skill can only read and produces less output.
`argument-hint`, so developers pass a narrower scope when they invoke it.
Nothing in the frontmatter; just run /compact after every use of the skill.
e: `context: fork` runs a skill in an isolated sub-agent context so its output doesn't pollute the main conversation, and the guide names verbose codebase analysis as the use case. Tool restrictions and argument hints don't isolate output.

q: A team skill should only be able to write files and must not run Bash or delete anything. How do you enforce this?
o: Set `allowed-tools` in the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter to only the file-writing tools.
Write "never run Bash or delete files" in bold at the top of the skill's instructions.
Set `context: fork` in the frontmatter so anything the skill does stays inside the sub-agent.
Add a section to the project CLAUDE.md describing which tools skills are allowed to use.
e: `allowed-tools` restricts tool access during skill execution, and the guide gives this exact use: limiting to file write operations to prevent destructive actions. `context: fork` isolates context, not side effects on disk.

q: Your `/migrate` skill needs a table name, but developers often run it with no arguments and get confusing results. What helps most?
o: Add `argument-hint` to the SKILL.md frontmatter so developers are prompted for the table name.
Add `context: fork` so the skill can ask the developer clarifying questions in isolation.
Hard-code a sensible default table name so the skill always has something to work with.
Document the required argument in the repository README and link it from CLAUDE.md.
e: `argument-hint` prompts developers for required parameters when they invoke the skill without arguments. A hard-coded default risks migrating the wrong table, and README notes aren't shown at invocation time.

q: You want your own tweaked version of the team's `deploy-check` skill without changing what teammates get. What should you do?
o: Create a personal variant in `~/.claude/skills/` with a different name.
Edit the skill in the repository's `.claude/skills/` folder.
Copy it into `~/.claude/skills/` with the same name so it takes over from the team version.
Ask teammates to stop using the shared skill.
e: The guide recommends personal variants in `~/.claude/skills/` with different names to avoid affecting teammates. Editing the repository version changes it for everyone, and reusing the same name invites confusion over which version runs.

q: Which split between skills and CLAUDE.md best follows the guide?
o: Always-on standards ("use TypeScript strict mode") go in CLAUDE.md; task workflows (release notes) become skills.
Put everything in CLAUDE.md, so Claude always has every instruction loaded in every session.
Make everything a skill, so CLAUDE.md stays empty and context is only used when needed.
Put standards in skills so they're invoked deliberately, and put workflows in CLAUDE.md.
e: CLAUDE.md is always loaded and suits universal standards. Skills are invoked on demand and suit task-specific workflows. Putting everything in CLAUDE.md wastes context, and making standards into skills means they only apply when someone remembers to invoke them.

q: Your Terraform conventions should apply only when Claude is editing Terraform files. What's the best setup?
o: A `.claude/rules/` file with YAML frontmatter `paths: ["terraform/**/*"]`.
A section at the top of the root CLAUDE.md titled "Terraform".
A `/terraform` slash command developers run first.
A `terraform.md` file in `~/.claude/`.
e: Rules in `.claude/rules/` with a `paths` glob load only when editing matching files. A root CLAUDE.md section loads for every task, and a slash command depends on someone remembering to run it.

q: What's the main advantage of path-scoped rules in `.claude/rules/`?
o: They load only when Claude edits matching files, which cuts irrelevant context and tokens.
They're compiled ahead of time, so they load and apply faster than CLAUDE.md instructions.
They take priority over every other instruction Claude receives, including the user's prompt.
They're excluded from version control by default, so each developer's rules stay private.
e: Path-scoped rules activate conditionally, so Claude only sees conventions relevant to the files it's working on. They're ordinary committed files and don't override everything.

q: Test files sit next to the code they test all over the codebase (`Button.test.tsx` beside `Button.tsx`). You want one set of testing conventions applied to all of them. What's best?
o: A `.claude/rules/` file with `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]`.
A CLAUDE.md file in every directory that contains tests.
A testing section in the root CLAUDE.md.
A testing skill that developers invoke before writing tests.
e: Glob-pattern rules apply conventions to files by type regardless of directory. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files are bound to one folder, so you'd need copies everywhere. Root CLAUDE.md loads them for every task, and skills need manual invocation.

q: Your API conventions must apply to `src/api/` and also to `services/*/handlers/`. What's the most maintainable approach?
o: One `.claude/rules/` file whose `paths` lists both glob patterns.
A CLAUDE.md in `src/api/` and a copy in each `services/*/handlers/` folder.
A note in root CLAUDE.md saying where the API code lives.
A personal rule in `~/.claude/` for each developer.
e: Path-specific rules beat subdirectory CLAUDE.md files when conventions span multiple directories: one file, several globs, no copies to keep in sync.

q: You need to add a date validation check to one function. The change is clear and small. Which approach fits?
o: Direct execution.
Plan mode, to explore the codebase first.
Plan mode, followed by an Explore subagent.
An interview pattern before any change.
e: Direct execution suits simple, well-scoped changes, and the guide uses "adding a date validation conditional" as its example. Plan mode adds overhead without benefit here.

q: You're migrating to a new library, which touches more than 45 files. What's the best workflow?
o: Use plan mode to investigate and design the migration, then direct execution to carry it out.
Start in direct execution and fix problems as they come up, since the migration steps are mechanical.
Stay in plan mode for the whole job, including every individual file change, to keep it safe.
Ask Claude to migrate all 45+ files in one direct-execution prompt with detailed instructions.
e: Large, multi-file changes call for plan mode, and the guide recommends combining plan mode for investigation with direct execution for implementation. Jumping straight in risks costly rework.

q: You must choose between two integration approaches that have different infrastructure requirements. Which mode fits?
o: Plan mode, since there are multiple valid approaches and architectural implications.
Direct execution, implementing the first approach and switching if it fails.
Direct execution with detailed instructions for both approaches.
Neither; decide without Claude's help.
e: Plan mode is designed for tasks with multiple valid approaches and architectural decisions, and the guide lists choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure needs as an example.

q: In a multi-phase task, the discovery phase produces huge amounts of output and your main context is filling fast. What helps most?
o: Use the Explore subagent for discovery, so verbose output stays isolated and only a summary returns.
Switch to direct execution for the rest of the task so the discovery phase can be skipped.
Paste the discovery output into CLAUDE.md so it's available later without filling the session.
Start a brand-new session for every phase, without carrying anything over between them.
e: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output and returns summaries, which prevents context exhaustion during multi-phase tasks. Skipping discovery or dropping everything between phases loses what you learned.

q: A bug report includes a clear stack trace pointing to one line in one file. Which approach fits?
o: Direct execution.
Plan mode, since all bugs deserve investigation first.
An Explore subagent to map the whole codebase.
A fork of the session to try several fixes.
e: The guide names "a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace" as a direct execution case. The scope is clear and plan mode would only add overhead.

q: You described a data transformation in prose, but Claude's output varies between runs. What's the most effective fix?
o: Give 2–3 concrete input/output examples of the transformation.
Rewrite the prose description to be longer and more detailed.
Ask Claude to be more consistent.
Lower the temperature to 0.
e: Concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate expected transformations when prose is interpreted inconsistently. More prose or a request for consistency doesn't remove the ambiguity.

q: You're building a pricing function with many edge cases. Which iteration approach does the guide recommend?
o: Write tests for behavior, edge cases, and performance first, then iterate by sharing test failures.
Have Claude write the function first, then write tests that check the behavior it produced.
Describe every edge case in one long paragraph and ask Claude for the finished function.
Ask Claude for five different versions and pick whichever one looks the most complete.
e: Test-driven iteration means writing tests first, then sharing failures to guide improvement. Tests written after the fact tend to confirm whatever the code already does.

q: You're adding a caching layer in a domain you don't know well. What should you do before Claude implements it?
o: Use the interview pattern: have Claude ask you about things like invalidation strategy and failure modes.
Ask Claude to implement the most widely used caching pattern for this kind of system right away.
Write the full specification yourself first, then hand it to Claude to implement exactly as written.
Implement the cache yourself, then ask Claude to review the finished code for problems.
e: The interview pattern has Claude ask questions that surface design considerations you may not have anticipated, such as cache invalidation and failure modes, before implementation.

q: You've found three bugs in a module, and fixing any one of them changes how the others behave. How should you raise them with Claude?
o: All in one detailed message, because the fixes interact.
One at a time, waiting for each fix before raising the next.
Only the most severe one; the others may disappear.
Each in a separate new session.
e: The guide says to address multiple interacting issues in a single detailed message, and to iterate sequentially only when issues are independent. Fixing interacting bugs one at a time causes churn.

q: Your migration script mishandles null values. What's the most effective way to get Claude to fix the edge case?
o: Give specific test cases with example input (including nulls) and the expected output.
Tell Claude to "handle null values properly" and run the script again.
Ask Claude to rewrite the whole migration script from scratch with nulls in mind.
Add a rule to CLAUDE.md saying all scripts must be null-safe.
e: The guide recommends specific test cases with example input and expected output to fix edge cases, using null handling in migration scripts as the example. A vague instruction leaves Claude guessing what "properly" means.

q: Your pipeline must post Claude Code's review findings as inline PR comments automatically. Which CLI options make the output machine-parseable?
o: `--output-format json` together with `--json-schema`
`--verbose` together with `--quiet`
Only `-p`, then parse the plain text with regular expressions
`--format markdown`
e: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` enforces structured output in CI, which you can then post as inline comments. Parsing free text with regular expressions is brittle.

q: After a developer pushes new commits, the re-run review posts duplicate comments for issues it already reported. What's the fix?
o: Include the prior findings in context and ask Claude to report only new or still-open issues.
Delete all of the previous review comments on the PR before each new review run starts.
Run the automated review only on the first commit of each PR, not on later pushes.
Raise the review's severity threshold so fewer and only the most serious issues get posted.
e: The guide's approach is to include prior findings and instruct Claude to report only new or unaddressed issues. Deleting comments loses discussion history, and reviewing only once misses new bugs.

q: Automated test generation keeps proposing tests the suite already has. What's the best fix?
o: Provide the existing test files in context so it avoids scenarios that are already covered.
Add an instruction asking Claude to be original and avoid obvious test cases.
Generate tests only for source files that currently have no tests at all.
Run a script after generation that filters out tests resembling existing ones.
e: Providing existing test files in context lets Claude see what's covered. A vague instruction can't help without that information, and filtering afterwards wastes generation effort.

q: CI-generated tests are mostly low-value (trivial getters) and ignore the team's fixtures. Where should you fix this?
o: Document testing standards, what makes a test valuable, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md.
Set the testing standards as environment variables in the CI runner's configuration.
Ask each developer to add the standards to their own `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` file.
Add a second generation pass in CI that replaces weak tests with stronger ones.
e: CLAUDE.md is how CI-invoked Claude Code gets project context such as testing standards, valuable test criteria, and fixtures. User-level files aren't present on the CI runner.

q: The same Claude Code session that generated a change is then asked to review it, and it misses obvious bugs. Why, and what's better?
o: It keeps its own generation reasoning and rarely questions it; use an independent review instance.
The session has run low on tokens by review time; raise `max_tokens` for the review step.
Reviews need a larger, more capable model than generation; switch models for the review.
The review prompt isn't strict enough; add "be very critical of this code" to the prompt.
e: Session context isolation matters: the generating session carries its reasoning and tends not to second-guess it. An independent instance without that context catches more. Asking for extra criticism doesn't remove the bias.

q: How does Claude Code running in CI learn your project's review criteria and testing conventions?
o: From the project's CLAUDE.md, which it reads in CI just like locally.
From the CI provider's settings page.
It can't; CI runs only see the diff.
From the user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` of whoever opened the PR.
e: The guide names CLAUDE.md as the mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude Code project context. The PR author's user-level file isn't on the CI machine.

q: Your review prompt says "check that comments are accurate." It flags dozens of harmless wording nitpicks per PR. What's the best rewrite?
o: "Flag a comment only when its claimed behavior contradicts what the code does."
"Check that comments are accurate, and be conservative about what you report as a problem."
"Only report comment issues that you are highly confident are real problems."
"Check comment accuracy, but limit yourself to five findings per PR."
e: Explicit criteria beat vague instructions; this is the guide's own example. "Be conservative" and confidence-based filtering don't improve precision, and a cap just drops findings at random.

q: You added "be conservative and only report high-confidence findings" to the review prompt, but false positives barely dropped. Why, and what works better?
o: Vague instructions like these don't raise precision; define which categories to report (bugs, security) and skip (style).
The wording isn't strong enough; change it to "be extremely conservative" and repeat it at the end of the prompt.
Confidence filtering needs a number to work; tell the model to report only findings above 90% confidence.
Prompting can't reduce false positives; filter findings afterwards with a separate classifier model instead.
e: The guide says general instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" fail compared to specific categorical criteria. Stronger adjectives or numeric confidence thresholds are the same idea dressed differently.

q: Your style-suggestion category has a 60% false positive rate, and developers have started ignoring all review comments, including accurate security findings. What should you do first?
o: Temporarily disable the high false-positive category to restore trust, while improving its prompt separately.
Keep everything on and add a note asking developers to read security findings carefully.
Turn off the whole automated review until every category is perfect.
Mark security findings in bold so they stand out.
e: High false-positive categories undermine trust in accurate ones. The guide recommends temporarily disabling them while improving their prompts. Shutting down the whole review loses the valuable categories too.

q: The reviewer labels similar issues "critical" in one PR and "minor" in another. How do you make severity consistent?
o: Define explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each level.
Tell the model to apply severity labels consistently across all PRs.
Drop severity labels and list every finding in one flat list.
Let developers relabel the severity of each finding after review.
e: The guide recommends explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples per level. A request for consistency doesn't define what each level means, and removing severity loses useful prioritization.

q: Your security findings are accurate, but a noisy style category produces lots of false positives. Why does the noisy category matter for the security findings?
o: Developers lose trust and start dismissing all findings, including accurate ones.
It doesn't matter much, because each category is judged by developers on its own.
The noisy category uses up context tokens that the security check would otherwise need.
Style findings change how the model rates the severity of the security findings.
e: The guide notes that high false positive categories undermine confidence in accurate categories. Trust is shared across the tool, so noise in one place hurts adoption everywhere.

q: You wrote detailed formatting instructions for review comments (location, issue, severity, suggested fix), but the output format still varies a lot. What's the most effective fix?
o: Add few-shot examples showing the exact output format you want.
Make the formatting instructions longer and more detailed.
Write the format rules in all caps.
Ask the model to double-check its formatting before answering.
e: Few-shot examples are the most effective technique for consistently formatted output when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results. More or louder instructions are what already wasn't working.

q: The reviewer keeps flagging an intentional, commented empty `catch` block that your team uses on purpose, while it correctly catches real swallowed errors. How do you cut these false positives without losing real findings?
o: Add few-shot examples contrasting the acceptable pattern with a genuine issue, so the model generalizes.
Add a rule telling the model to ignore every empty `catch` block it sees from now on.
Remove error handling from the review criteria entirely, since it causes the false positives.
Add the affected files to an ignore list so the reviewer skips them on future PRs.
e: Few-shot examples distinguishing acceptable patterns from genuine issues reduce false positives while enabling generalization. Blanket ignore rules would also hide the real bugs.

q: Your extraction returns null for required fields when values appear in a table instead of in narrative text. What's the most effective fix?
o: Add few-shot examples showing correct extraction from varied formats, including tables.
Make those fields optional so a null result is allowed and no longer fails validation.
Tell the model to "look harder" and check every part of the document for each value.
Convert every table into prose before extraction so all values appear the same way.
e: The guide recommends few-shot examples showing correct extraction from documents with varied formats to address empty or null extraction of required fields. Making the fields optional hides the miss rather than fixing it.

q: Recipe documents use informal measurements ("a good handful," "about a cup and a half"), and the extractor sometimes invents precise values. What helps most?
o: Few-shot examples demonstrating how to handle informal measurements correctly.
A rule saying "never hallucinate."
A lower `max_tokens` setting.
Requiring every quantity field so the model always fills it.
e: The guide notes few-shot examples are effective for reducing hallucination in extraction tasks, naming informal measurements specifically. Making fields required pushes the model toward fabricating values.

q: The model handles clear review cases well but struggles with ambiguous ones. What kind of few-shot examples should you add?
o: 2–4 targeted ambiguous cases, each showing why one action beat the plausible alternatives.
20 or more examples covering every case you can think of, so nothing is left unclear.
Several examples of the clear-cut cases, since those show the model the ideal behavior.
A single example showing the final answer only, to keep the prompt short and focused.
e: The guide recommends 2–4 targeted few-shot examples for ambiguous scenarios that show reasoning for the chosen action versus alternatives. Dozens of examples add tokens, and clear-cut examples don't teach the hard boundary.

q: Research papers cite sources in different ways: some use inline citations, others put everything in a bibliography. Your citation extraction misses one style. What's the fix?
o: Few-shot examples showing correct extraction from both inline-citation and bibliography papers.
Only process papers that use inline citations, and route the others to manual review.
Tell the model which citation style each paper uses before it starts extracting.
Make the citations field optional so papers with the other style don't fail validation.
e: The guide uses this exact case: few-shot examples demonstrating correct handling of varied document structures, like inline citations versus bibliographies.

q: Why do few-shot examples often outperform a long list of explicit rules for review judgment?
o: They help the model generalize judgment to new patterns, not just the cases you listed.
Examples always use fewer tokens than an equivalent list of written rules.
The model tends to ignore rule lists that run longer than about a page.
Examples turn off the model's own judgment so it copies them exactly.
e: Few-shot examples enable generalization to novel patterns rather than matching only pre-specified cases, which rule lists struggle to do.

q: What's the most reliable way to get schema-compliant JSON from Claude for extraction?
o: Define an extraction tool whose input schema is your JSON schema and use `tool_use`.
Ask in the prompt for "valid JSON only, no other text."
Let Claude answer freely and extract the JSON with a regular expression.
Ask for JSON inside a markdown code block.
e: Tool use with JSON schemas is the most reliable approach to guaranteed schema-compliant output and eliminates JSON syntax errors. Prompt requests and regex parsing can still break.

q: Your pipeline has separate extraction tools for invoices, receipts, and contracts, and you don't know a document's type in advance. You must always get structured output. Which setting fits?
o: `tool_choice: "any"`
`tool_choice: "auto"`
`tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}`
No tools; ask for JSON in the prompt instead.
e: "any" guarantees the model calls a tool while letting it choose the right schema for the document. "auto" may return text, and forcing `extract_invoice` would misfile receipts and contracts.

q: You use `tool_use` with a strict schema, yet some invoices come back with line items that don't add up to the total. Why?
o: Strict schemas stop syntax errors, not semantic ones; you still need checks like calculated vs stated totals.
The schema isn't strict enough yet; adding more required fields will make the totals add up.
Tool use only produces reliable output for documents shorter than one page.
The model can't do arithmetic reliably, so totals should be removed from the schema.
e: The guide stresses that schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but don't prevent semantic errors such as line items not summing to the total, or values in the wrong fields.

q: Some purchase orders don't include a PO number. The field is `required` in your schema, and the model has started inventing PO numbers. What's the fix?
o: Make the field optional (nullable) so the model can return null when it's missing.
Add "never invent PO numbers" to the prompt in bold, at the top and bottom.
Reject every document without a PO number before it reaches extraction.
Retry extraction until a real-looking PO number appears in the output.
e: Optional or nullable fields prevent the model from fabricating values to satisfy required fields. Retrying can't produce information that isn't in the document.

q: Your `category` enum is ["electronics", "apparel", "home"]. New product types get forced into the wrong category, and some items are genuinely ambiguous. What's the better schema design?
