o: Add "other" with a detail string for new categories, and "unclear" for ambiguous items.
Remove the enum and accept any free-text category the model wants to write.
Keep adding new enum values each time a new product type shows up in the data.
Make the category field required so the model always commits to one of the three.
e: The guide recommends "other" + detail fields for extensible categorization and "unclear" for ambiguous cases. Free text loses consistency, and constant enum changes are never complete.

q: Source documents write dates as "3/4/25," "March 4th, 2025," and "2025-03-04," and your extracted dates are inconsistent. What should you add?
o: Add normalization rules to the prompt (such as "output ISO 8601") alongside the strict schema.
Nothing extra; the schema's `string` type already makes the extracted dates consistent.
Define a separate extraction tool for each of the input date formats you've seen.
Tell the model to skip any date that isn't already written in ISO 8601 format.
e: The guide recommends including format normalization rules in prompts alongside strict output schemas to handle inconsistent source formatting. A string type accepts any format.

q: With `tool_choice` set to "auto", some responses contain only text and no extraction tool call. Why?
o: "auto" lets the model reply in text instead; use "any" or force the tool.
The extraction tool's JSON schema is invalid, so the model can't call it.
"auto" only works reliably when there's exactly one tool defined.
Those responses hit `max_tokens` before the model reached the tool call.
e: "auto" means the model may return text instead of calling a tool. "any" requires a tool call, and forced selection requires a specific tool.

q: You defined an `extract_invoice` tool with a JSON schema and the model called it. Where is the structured data?
o: In the `input` of the `tool_use` block.
In a text block after the tool call.
In a `tool_result` block in the response.
In the response's `stop_reason` field.
e: For extraction, you define the tool with a JSON schema as its input parameters and read the structured data from the `tool_use` block's input. You don't need to run anything; the arguments are the extraction.

q: An extraction fails validation because a date came back in the wrong format. How should you design the retry?
o: Send the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error.
Resend the exact same request and hope the next attempt comes out differently.
Send only the validation error message, without the document, to save tokens.
Switch to a different model for each retry until one passes validation.
e: Retry-with-error-feedback includes the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific errors. A blind retry gives the model nothing new, and without the document it can't fix the value properly.

q: Retries keep failing on a contract's "termination date." You discover that date only appears in a separate amendment that isn't part of the input. What should you do?
o: Stop retrying: the value isn't in the input, so return null or flag it (or supply the amendment).
Keep retrying with stronger wording that insists the model find the termination date.
Retry with a higher temperature so the model explores other parts of the document.
Make the field required in the schema so the model has to provide some value.
e: Retries are ineffective when the information is absent from the source. They help for format or structural errors, not missing data. Forcing a value invites fabrication.

q: Developers dismiss a lot of review findings, and you want to learn which kinds of code trigger the dismissed ones. What should you add to each finding?
o: A `detected_pattern` field naming the code construct that triggered it.
A field recording the name of the developer who dismissed the finding.
A free-text field where the model explains how confident it is in the finding and why.
A timestamp recording when each finding was created.
e: The guide's feedback loop design adds `detected_pattern` to findings so you can systematically analyze which constructs drive dismissals and false positives.

q: How can the extraction itself help catch invoices whose line items don't match the stated total?
o: Extract a `calculated_total` next to the `stated_total`, plus a `conflict_detected` flag.
Extract only the stated total and trust it, since it's printed on the invoice itself.
Ask the model in a follow-up message whether it's sure about the total it extracted.
Remove line items from the schema so there's nothing to disagree with the total.
e: Self-correction flows extract both calculated and stated totals so discrepancies are flagged, plus `conflict_detected` booleans for inconsistent source data.

q: Which extraction failure is most likely to be fixed by a retry with error feedback?
o: The model put a valid date in the wrong output format.
The required value appears only in an attachment that wasn't provided.
The scanned document is missing the page with the totals.
The customer's name is not in the document at all.
e: Format mismatches and structural output errors respond well to retry with feedback. When information is absent from the source, no amount of retrying will produce it.

q: Every night you need to extract data from 10,000 documents for a report people read the next morning. What's the most cost-effective approach?
o: The Message Batches API, for about 50% savings; the job can wait up to 24 hours.
Parallel synchronous API calls, so the results arrive as quickly as possible.
A few documents each hour through the synchronous API, spread across the night.
An interactive Claude Code session left running overnight to work through them.
e: The Batches API saves about 50% and suits non-blocking, latency-tolerant work like overnight reports. Synchronous calls cost more and the speed isn't needed.

q: Documents must be processed within 30 hours of arrival. Batches can take up to 24 hours. How often should you submit batches?
o: Every 4 hours.
Every 8 hours.
Every 12 hours.
Once a day.
e: A document can wait up to one submission interval before its batch starts, then up to 24 hours to process. Interval + 24 must stay under 30, so the interval must be under 6 hours; the guide's example uses 4-hour windows. 8, 12, or 24 hours could all miss the SLA.

q: In a batch of 500 documents, 12 failed because they exceeded context limits. What's the best recovery?
o: Resubmit only those 12, found by `custom_id`, after splitting them into chunks.
Resubmit the whole batch of 500 unchanged so every result comes from one run.
Resubmit the 12 failures unchanged, since batch errors are often temporary.
Leave the 12 out of the report and note how many documents were skipped.
e: Handle batch failures by resubmitting only the failed items (found by `custom_id`) with the right modification, here chunking oversized documents. Resubmitting all 500 wastes money, and unchanged resubmissions fail again.

q: Your extraction workflow calls a lookup tool mid-request to fetch reference data, then continues extracting. Can you move it to the Message Batches API as it is?
o: No: batches can't run tools mid-request, so pre-fetch the reference data into the prompt or stay synchronous.
Yes: batch requests can run tools and continue, exactly the same way synchronous requests do.
Yes, as long as every request in the batch carries its own unique `custom_id`.
Yes, but the tool calls are queued and run only after the whole batch has completed.
e: The batch API can't execute tools mid-request and return results. Work that needs that must be restructured or stay on the synchronous API.

q: You're about to batch-process 50,000 documents with a new extraction prompt. What should you do first?
o: Refine the prompt on a sample set first to maximize first-pass success.
Submit all 50,000 right away and fix whatever fails once results come back.
Split them into 50 batches and adjust the prompt a little between each one.
Run the first 10,000 through the synchronous API, then batch the rest.
e: The guide recommends prompt refinement on a sample set before large batches, which raises first-pass success and cuts resubmission costs.

q: How do you match each batch result to the document it came from?
o: Give each request a `custom_id` and use it to correlate the responses.
Rely on results coming back in the same order you submitted them.
Ask the model to repeat the document's filename in its output.
Submit one document per batch.
e: `custom_id` fields correlate batch request/response pairs. Relying on order or on the model echoing names is fragile, and one document per batch loses the efficiency.

q: After generating code, you add "now critically review your own code" in the same session. It rarely finds anything, but a later human review finds several bugs. What's the better design?
o: Use a second, independent Claude instance without the generator's reasoning to review the code.
Make the self-review instruction more forceful, telling it to assume the code has bugs.
Ask for self-review three times in a row and combine whatever each pass finds.
Turn on extended thinking in the same session so the self-review reasons more deeply.
e: A model that keeps its generation reasoning is less likely to question its own decisions. Independent review instances catch subtle issues better than self-review instructions or extended thinking.

q: Which review setup is most likely to catch subtle bugs in generated code?
o: An independent review instance that has no access to the generator's reasoning.
The same session, reviewing with extended thinking turned on.
The same session, told to pretend it's a different reviewer.
The generator, reviewing its code right after writing each function.
e: The guide states independent instances (without prior reasoning context) are more effective at catching subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking. Role-play doesn't remove the shared context.

q: You want high-confidence review findings posted automatically and uncertain ones sent to a human for triage. What should you add?
o: A verification pass with per-finding confidence, using thresholds checked against labeled examples.
Post every finding automatically and let developers dismiss the ones they disagree with.
Send every finding to human triage first, so nothing is posted without being checked.
Keep only findings that show up in at least two out of three identical review runs.
e: The guide describes verification passes with per-finding self-reported confidence to enable calibrated review routing, and calibrating thresholds on labeled data keeps that routing honest. Consensus voting suppresses real bugs that are only caught intermittently.

q: In a long support chat, progressive summarization turned "refund of $247.83 for order #8812, promised by Friday" into "customer wants a refund." The agent later gets the amount and deadline wrong. What's the fix?
o: Keep a persistent "case facts" block (amounts, dates, order IDs, statuses) in every prompt, outside the summary.
Summarize less often, for example every 20 turns instead of every 5, so fewer details get compressed.
Have the agent ask the customer to repeat the key details whenever they become relevant again.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so summarization is needed much less often.
e: Progressive summarization tends to blur numbers, dates, and customer expectations. The guide's fix is extracting transactional facts into a persistent case-facts block included with each prompt. Summarizing less often only delays the loss.

q: The synthesis agent receives one long input with 20 subagent findings. Findings in the middle are often left out of the report. What's happening, and what helps?
o: The "lost in the middle" effect; lead with a key-findings summary and use clear section headers.
The input hit the token limit, so the middle was cut; raise `max_tokens` for synthesis.
The middle findings tend to be lower quality, so it's reasonable to drop them from the input.
The ordering is the problem, so shuffle the findings randomly on each run to spread the loss.
e: Models reliably process the beginning and end of long inputs but may omit the middle. The guide recommends key findings summaries at the beginning and explicit section headers. Shuffling just moves which findings get lost.

q: Each `lookup_order` call returns more than 40 fields, but returns handling only needs about 5. The context fills up quickly in long sessions. What's the best fix?
o: Trim each tool output to the fields that matter (such as the return-related ones) before it enters context.
Summarize the whole conversation every few turns so old tool results take up less space.
Move to a model with a larger context window so the full order records fit comfortably.
Tell the model in the system prompt to ignore the order fields it doesn't need.
e: Tool results accumulate and consume tokens out of proportion to their relevance. Trimming verbose outputs to the needed fields before they accumulate is the guide's fix; a PostToolUse hook is a natural place to do it.

q: Your chat app sends only the newest customer message with each API request. Claude keeps losing track of what was already discussed. What's wrong?
o: Each request must include the complete conversation history.
The system prompt is too short to keep Claude oriented.
Claude needs a separate memory tool to recall earlier turns.
The temperature is too high, so replies drift between turns.
e: The API doesn't remember previous requests on its own. The guide stresses passing complete conversation history in later requests to maintain coherence.

q: The synthesis agent has a tight context budget, but upstream agents send it long reasoning chains and raw page text. What's the best change?
o: Have upstream agents return structured data (key facts, citations, relevance scores) instead of verbose text.
Give the synthesis agent a larger model so it can handle the longer inputs it receives.
Have the synthesis agent read only the first half of each input to stay within budget.
Tell the synthesis agent to skim each input and focus only on what looks important.
e: The guide recommends modifying upstream agents to return structured data instead of verbose content when downstream agents have limited context budgets. Truncating or skimming drops information at random.

q: A customer raises issues on three different orders in one session, and the agent starts mixing up their amounts and statuses. What should you do?
o: Keep each issue's structured data (order ID, amount, status) in a separate, persistent context layer.
Limit the agent to one order per session and ask the customer to start new chats for the others.
Re-run `lookup_order` for all three orders before every reply so the data is always fresh.
Ask the customer which order they mean at the start of every message.
e: For multi-issue sessions, the guide recommends extracting and persisting structured issue data in a separate context layer so details don't blur together.

q: A customer opens with: "I want to talk to a human, please." Their issue looks simple. What should the agent do?
o: Escalate to a human right away, without investigating first.
Fix the issue first, since it's simple, then offer a human if they still want one.
Explain that the agent can handle it and ask them to continue.
Ask why they want a human before deciding.
e: Honor explicit requests for a human immediately, without first attempting investigation. Overriding a clear preference damages trust even when the issue looks easy.

q: A frustrated customer writes, "This is ridiculous, my package is late AGAIN." They haven't asked for a human, and the delay is something the agent can fix. What's the best response?
o: Acknowledge the frustration and offer to fix it; escalate only if they then ask for a human.
Escalate to a human right away, because the customer is clearly upset.
Skip past the tone and reply only with the tracking details for the package.
Offer a discount code as an apology and close the conversation.
e: The guide says to acknowledge frustration while offering resolution when the issue is within the agent's ability, escalating only if the customer states a preference for a human. Frustration alone isn't an escalation trigger.

q: A customer asks you to match a competitor's lower price. Your policy covers price adjustments for your own site's sales but says nothing about competitors. What should the agent do?
o: Escalate to a human, because the policy is silent on this request.
Approve the match, since own-site adjustments are allowed.
Refuse, since competitor matching isn't listed.
Ask the customer for proof and then approve it.
e: Escalate when policy is ambiguous or silent on the specific request; competitor price matching is the guide's own example. Guessing in either direction makes a policy decision the agent isn't authorized to make.

q: `get_customer` returns three matches for "John Smith." What should the agent do?
o: Ask the customer for another identifier, such as email or order number.
Pick the account with the most recent order, since it's most likely active.
Pick the first match returned, since lookups are sorted by relevance.
Continue with all three accounts and narrow it down later in the chat.
e: Multiple matches require clarification with additional identifiers, not heuristic selection. Picking by recency or position risks acting on the wrong account.

q: Why is sentiment-based escalation a weak strategy?
o: Sentiment doesn't track how complex a case is, so it escalates the wrong cases.
Running sentiment analysis on every message is too expensive at scale.
Customers are rarely upset enough to trigger a sentiment threshold.
It always escalates too few cases to make a measurable difference.
e: Sentiment is an unreliable proxy for case complexity. Angry customers can have simple issues, and calm ones can have policy exceptions. The guide lists sentiment and self-reported confidence as unreliable proxies.

q: Which set of escalation triggers matches the guide?
o: The customer asks for a human, a policy exception or gap, or no meaningful progress.
Any case that needs more than three tool calls to resolve.
Any customer message that shows negative sentiment.
Any time the agent's self-rated confidence drops below 7 out of 10.
e: Appropriate triggers are explicit requests for a human, policy exceptions or gaps (not just complex cases), and inability to progress. Tool-call counts, sentiment, and self-reported confidence are poor proxies.

q: One of four source databases was unavailable during research, so the report's section on that area is thin. How should synthesis handle it?
o: Add coverage annotations showing which findings are well supported and which areas have gaps.
Fill the thin section from the model's general knowledge so the report reads as complete.
Quietly leave the thin area out of the report so it doesn't look unbalanced.
Fail the whole report and rerun it once the missing database is back online.
e: The guide recommends structuring synthesis output with coverage annotations showing well-supported findings versus gaps from unavailable sources, so readers know where the report is thin.

q: A search subagent's niche query returns zero results. Another subagent's query times out. How should each be reported to the coordinator?
o: Zero results as a successful search with no matches; the timeout as an access failure with context.
Both as errors, so the coordinator retries both queries with the same parameters.
Both as successful empty results, to keep the coordinator's logic as simple as possible.
Neither; each subagent should handle both cases on its own without telling the coordinator.
e: Distinguishing access failures from valid empty results lets the coordinator decide correctly: rephrase or accept a real "nothing found," and retry or reroute a timeout.

q: The document analysis subagent fails on 1 of 12 documents, and right now the entire research workflow aborts. What's the better design?
o: Return a structured error plus the partial results from the other 11, and let the coordinator decide.
Keep aborting the workflow, since an incomplete report is worse than producing none at all.
Skip the failed document silently and report the analysis step as fully successful.
Retry the failing document in a loop until it eventually succeeds, however long it takes.
e: Terminating entire workflows on single failures and silently suppressing errors are both anti-patterns. Structured errors with partial results let the coordinator recover intelligently.

q: Two hours into exploring a large codebase, Claude starts referring to "typical patterns" instead of the specific classes it found earlier, and its answers become inconsistent. What helps most?
o: Keep a scratchpad file of key findings and refer back to it.
Ask Claude to concentrate harder on remembering earlier results.
Keep going; it will recover after it reads more of the files.
Raise the temperature so it explores more varied answers.
e: This is context degradation in extended sessions. Scratchpad files persist key findings across context boundaries so Claude can rely on them instead of fading memory.

q: Your Claude Code session's context is filling up with verbose discovery output, and you're not done exploring. Which command helps?
o: `/compact`
`/memory`
`--resume`
e: `/compact` reduces context usage during long exploration sessions. `/memory` shows loaded memory files, `-p` runs non-interactively, and `--resume` continues a prior session.

q: The main agent needs answers to "find all test files" and "trace the refund flow's dependencies" without its context filling with search output. What should it do?
o: Spawn subagents for each question that return summaries, while the main agent keeps coordinating.
Run both searches in the main context, then summarize the results at the end.
Ask the user to answer both questions, since they likely know the codebase.
Read the whole repository into the main context first so both answers are on hand.
e: Subagent delegation isolates verbose exploration output while the main agent preserves high-level coordination; the guide uses these exact example questions.

q: Your long-running multi-agent job sometimes crashes partway, and restarting means redoing everything. What design enables recovery?
o: Each agent exports state to a known location; on resume the coordinator loads a manifest and injects it.
Restart from scratch on a machine with more memory so the job is less likely to crash.
Keep each agent's state only in its conversation history, which persists between runs.
Run only one agent at a time so a crash never affects more than one piece of work.
e: Structured state persistence for crash recovery: agents export state to known locations, and the coordinator loads a manifest on resume. Conversation history disappears with the crash.

q: You've finished the discovery phase of a big refactor and are about to spawn subagents for the implementation phase. What should you do first?
o: Summarize the discovery findings and inject that summary into the new subagents' context.
Let each new subagent rediscover what it needs, so it builds its own understanding.
Pass the full raw discovery transcript to every subagent so nothing is lost.
Nothing; the new subagents inherit the parent's context automatically when spawned.
e: The guide recommends summarizing findings from one phase before spawning subagents for the next and injecting the summaries. Subagents don't inherit parent context, and raw transcripts waste their context.

q: Your extraction system shows 97% overall accuracy, and management wants to remove human review. What should you check first?
o: Accuracy by document type and field, since the overall number can hide weak segments.
Nothing more; 97% is above any reasonable threshold for removing review.
Whether the pipeline is fast enough to run without the review step.
Overall accuracy again on a second, larger test set to confirm it.
e: Aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance on specific document types or fields (handwritten receipts, for example). Validate by segment before automating. A bigger aggregate number has the same blind spot.

q: High-confidence extractions are now auto-approved. How do you keep measuring their error rate and spot new kinds of errors?
o: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for ongoing review.
Reviewing only the extractions that customers or users complain about.
Trusting the confidence scores, since high confidence means the extraction is correct.
Running each extraction twice and flagging any that come out different.
e: Stratified random sampling measures error rates in high-confidence extractions and detects novel error patterns. Complaint-driven review is biased, and confidence alone isn't proof of correctness.

q: You want field-level confidence scores to decide which extractions go to human review. How do you set the thresholds?
o: Output field-level confidence, then calibrate thresholds on a labeled validation set.
Use a fixed 0.9 confidence threshold for every field in every document type.
Use the model's raw confidence scores directly, without any calibration step.
Let the reviewers set thresholds for each field based on their experience.
e: Field-level confidence must be calibrated using labeled validation sets to be useful for routing. Raw or arbitrary thresholds aren't tied to actual accuracy.

q: Reviewer capacity is limited. Which extractions should go to human review first?
o: Low-confidence extractions and ambiguous or contradictory sources.
An equally weighted random sample of all extractions.
The newest documents, since they reflect current formats.
The longest documents, since they have the most fields.
e: The guide recommends routing low-confidence extractions and ambiguous or contradictory sources to humans to make the best use of limited capacity. Random sampling is for measurement, not prioritization.

q: Two credible sources report different figures for the same statistic (32% and 41%). How should the system handle this?
o: Report both values with attribution and annotate the conflict.
Use the average of the two values, 36.5%, in the report.
Use whichever value appears in more of the sources found.
Leave the statistic out of the report to avoid confusion.
e: The guide says to annotate conflicting statistics with source attribution instead of arbitrarily selecting one. Averaging invents a number neither source reported.

q: After the summarization step, the final report can no longer say which source backs which claim. What's the fix?
o: Require structured claim-source mappings (URL, document, excerpt) that synthesis must keep and merge.
Ask the report agent to add a list of citations at the end, matched to claims as best it can.
Skip the summarization step entirely so the full source text reaches the report agent.
Cite every source next to every claim, so no claim is ever left without a citation.
e: Attribution is lost when findings are compressed without claim-source mappings. Structured mappings that downstream agents preserve keep provenance intact. Citing everything everywhere is meaningless.

q: Your report flags a "contradiction" between two statistics, but one is from 2019 and the other from 2024. How do you prevent this?
o: Require subagents to include publication or collection dates in their output.
Always keep only the most recent source and discard older figures.
Tell the synthesis agent to ignore apparent contradictions between sources.
Average the two figures so the report shows a single stable value.
e: Requiring dates in structured outputs prevents temporal differences from being misread as contradictions. Discarding older data or ignoring conflicts loses real information.

q: Your synthesis output turns everything (financial figures, news, and technical findings) into uniform bullet points. What does the guide recommend?
o: Render each type appropriately: financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as lists.
Keep everything as bullet points, since a single format is easiest to skim.
Write everything as flowing prose, since reports read best as narrative.
Put everything in one large table, so every finding can be compared side by side.
e: The guide recommends rendering different content types appropriately in synthesis outputs rather than converting everything to one format.

q: While analyzing a report, the document analysis subagent finds that the summary table and the body text give different revenue numbers. What should it do?
o: Finish with both values included and the conflict annotated, and let the coordinator reconcile.
Use the number from the summary table, since tables are usually more precise than body text.
Stop the analysis and return an error, since the document can't be trusted.
Leave both revenue numbers out, so no wrong figure reaches the final report.
e: The guide says to complete document analysis with conflicting values included and annotated, letting the coordinator decide before synthesis. The subagent shouldn't silently resolve conflicts it can't judge.

q: Your report mixes settled findings with ones that sources dispute, all in the same confident tone. How should you structure it?
o: Separate well-established from contested findings in explicit sections, keeping each source's framing.
Remove the contested findings so the report only states what is certain.
Add "this may be disputed" after every finding so readers stay appropriately cautious.
Present only the findings from the most-cited source, since it's the most authoritative.
e: The guide recommends structuring reports with explicit sections distinguishing well-established from contested findings, preserving source characterizations. Blanket caveats or removal both hide what readers need to know.

q: Your CI job runs `claude -p` and needs a team-specific reviewer persona, but you still want Claude Code's built-in tool guidance and safety instructions. Which flag fits?
o: `--append-system-prompt`, which adds your text to the end of the default system prompt.
`--system-prompt`, which swaps the default system prompt for your reviewer persona text.
`--output-format json`, which makes the reviewer follow a structured persona definition.
`--resume`, which reloads a saved session that already contains the reviewer persona.
e: `--append-system-prompt` (or `--append-system-prompt-file`) adds to the default prompt and keeps its tool guidance, safety instructions and coding conventions. `--system-prompt` replaces the entire default prompt, dropping all of that. Output format and session resumption don't define a persona.

q: Your CI runner has leftover hooks, plugins and local MCP servers configured, so scripted `claude -p` calls start slowly and behave differently from run to run. What helps most?
o: Run with `--bare`, which skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md, and pass needed context explicitly.
Run with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, so leftover hooks can't stop the job with prompts.
Run with `--system-prompt` so the default prompt, and everything it loads, is replaced.
Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude to ignore any hooks and plugins it finds.
e: `--bare` is minimal mode: it skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md so scripted calls start faster and more predictably. Because CLAUDE.md is skipped too, give the job its context explicitly. Skipping permissions doesn't stop hooks or plugins from loading, and a system prompt can't unload them.

q: A teammate wants `--dangerously-skip-permissions` on the shared CI runner, which holds deploy credentials, so jobs never stall on permission prompts. What's the best response?
o: Pre-approve only the tools the job needs (for example with `--allowedTools`) and keep bypass mode for isolated sandboxes with nothing sensitive.
Agree, since `-p` runs are non-interactive and the flag only removes prompts nobody would answer anyway.
Agree, but also add a CLAUDE.md note asking Claude to avoid touching the deploy credentials.
Refuse, because Claude Code can't run in CI at all without a person approving each tool call.
e: `--dangerously-skip-permissions` is equivalent to bypassPermissions mode: every permission prompt is skipped, so nothing stops a harmful action on a machine with secrets. Allow-listing just the needed tools removes the stalls without opening everything. A CLAUDE.md note is only guidance, and CI use doesn't require a person per call.

q: You use Claude's managed Code Review on GitHub. You want reviews to flag missing migration rollbacks as high severity and to skip generated files, without changing how Claude Code behaves on other tasks. Where do these rules go?
o: In a REVIEW.md file at the repository root.
In the project CLAUDE.md, under a section for reviews.
In a `.claude/commands/review.md` slash command file.
In the description of each pull request you want reviewed.
e: REVIEW.md holds instructions for reviews alone: what to flag, at what severity, and what to skip. CLAUDE.md is read for every task, reviews included, so review-only rules there would leak into other work. A slash command isn't what the managed review reads, and PR descriptions would need repeating every time.

q: A pull request edits REVIEW.md to drop the rule that flags unsafe SQL, and its own managed review still flags unsafe SQL. Why?
o: Code Review reads REVIEW.md from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's own changes.
Review rules only reload once a day, so the change will apply to tomorrow's reviews.
CLAUDE.md always overrides REVIEW.md, and it still contains the SQL rule.
Edits to REVIEW.md only take effect after someone comments `@claude review` twice.
e: REVIEW.md is read from the base or default branch, so a pull request can't loosen the rules for its own review. Protecting the default branch controls which copy is honored. There's no daily reload or comment-count rule.

q: An MCP server your team uses exposes several prompts (for example `summarize_incident`). How do developers use them in Claude Code?
o: They appear as slash commands named like `/mcp__<server>__<prompt>`.
Claude Code adds every MCP prompt to the system prompt at startup.
They must first be copied by hand into `.claude/commands/` files.
They can only be called from code through the Agent SDK, not interactively.
e: MCP servers can expose prompts, and Claude Code surfaces them as slash commands in the form `/mcp__<server>__<prompt>`, available alongside the server's tools. They aren't injected into the system prompt and don't need copying into command files.

q: `process_refund` times out after the request was sent. You can't tell whether the refund went through, and a blind retry could refund the customer twice. What should the tool and agent do?
o: Treat it as an ambiguous outcome: check the refund's status (or retry with the same idempotency key) before any new attempt.
Mark it as a transient error with `isRetryable: true` so the agent simply calls `process_refund` again.
Mark it as a permanent failure and tell the customer the refund couldn't be processed.
Report success to the customer, since most timeouts happen after the work is already done.
e: A timeout on a non-idempotent action is neither a clean success nor a clean failure. The safe pattern is to verify state (or reuse an idempotency key so a repeat can't double-charge) before trying again. Blind retries risk duplicate refunds, while declaring failure or success without checking can mislead the customer.

q: Your support agent's loop is capped with `max_turns`. When the cap is hit, some customers are left with neither a resolution nor a handoff. What's the most reliable fix?
o: In the orchestration code, detect a loop that ended on the turn limit and trigger an escalation with a structured handoff summary.
Tell the agent in its system prompt to escalate before it runs out of turns.
Raise `max_turns` high enough that conversations almost never reach it.
Remove `max_turns` entirely so the agent can keep working until it finishes.
e: Running out of turns is a code-level event, so code should guarantee what happens next: hand off with customer ID, root cause, what was tried and the recommended action. The model can't reliably count its remaining turns, a higher cap only makes the gap rarer, and removing the cap trades the problem for runaway loops.

q: Before refunds, your agent asks reviewers "Approve this refund? (yes/no)". Reviewers approve almost everything within seconds, and several wrong refunds got through. What's the best fix?
o: Show the full details in the confirmation (customer, order, amount, reason, and that it can't be undone) so reviewers can actually check it.
Add a second "Are you sure?" prompt after the first approval.
Require reviewers to wait 30 seconds before the approve button works.
Remove the confirmation step, since reviewers aren't adding any value.
e: A bare yes/no prompt invites rubber-stamping because there's nothing to check. Putting the specific facts in front of the reviewer turns the approval into a real verification. Extra prompts and delays add friction without information, and removing the step loses the safeguard.

q: When a request is ambiguous, your assistant replies with five clarifying questions at once, and many customers abandon the chat. What's a better pattern?
o: Ask one focused clarifying question at a time, starting with the one that most changes what to do next.
Skip clarifying questions and guess the most likely meaning every time.
Keep all five questions but format them as a numbered list.
Escalate any ambiguous request to a human right away.
e: One targeted question at a time keeps the conversation easy to answer and often resolves the ambiguity in a single step. Guessing risks acting on the wrong reading, a tidier list is still a wall of questions, and ambiguity alone isn't an escalation trigger.

q: After 60 turns, your assistant's replies slow down and it starts contradicting details the customer gave early on. Most of the context is old, verbose tool output. What's the best fix?
o: Trim stale tool outputs and older turns, while keeping a structured block of key facts and the most recent turns verbatim.
Start a brand-new conversation every 20 turns with no carry-over.
Ask the customer to restate their key details every few turns.
Move to a model with a larger context window and keep everything.
e: Verbose, stale context dilutes attention and costs tokens. Trimming it while preserving key facts and recent turns keeps the assistant accurate. Restarting loses facts, asking customers to repeat themselves is a poor experience, and a bigger window doesn't fix diluted attention.

q: One source gives a pricing table and another gives a regulator's exact statement. Your synthesis paraphrases both into smooth prose, and readers can no longer check the numbers or the wording. What should change?
o: Keep each source's format: carry the table through as a table and the statement as a verbatim, attributed quote.
Paraphrase everything for a consistent voice, and list the sources at the end.
Drop the table and the quote, and summarize only the overall conclusion.
Convert everything, including the quote, into one comparison table.
e: Preserving each source's form keeps precision and lets readers verify: tables stay tables, exact statements stay quoted with attribution. Uniform paraphrase or a single format loses exactly the details that matter.

q: Your weekly batch extraction feeds a trend dashboard, so results must stay comparable week to week. Halfway through the quarter, someone switches the job to a newer model and tweaks the prompt. What should the process require?
o: Pin the exact model version and a versioned prompt for the whole series, and re-baseline on a sample before switching either.
Always use the newest model as soon as it's available, since newer models are more accurate.
Let each week's job choose its own model and prompt, then average the results.
Switch models freely but keep the same `custom_id` values so results line up.
e: Changing the model or prompt mid-series changes the measurement, so trends start reflecting the pipeline instead of the data. Pin both, and when you do upgrade, rerun a sample to re-baseline. `custom_id` only correlates requests with responses.
